materials.text: Herd knowledge, coordinated movement and food/hide processing made the hunt more than a moment at the cliff.

knowledge.text: Blackfoot accounts locate bison within social and spiritual responsibilities; other Plains communities had distinct histories.

custody.text: Layers, landscape and limited experiments test different questions; no one photograph recovers an entire hunt.

name: Blackfoot bison knowledge and the work of a communal hunt
place: Head-Smashed-In, southern Alberta; wider Blackfoot cultural context
geographicPrecision: One communal-hunting landscape, not all Blackfoot territory or every Plains society. Earlier site users are not assigned an individual identity from a landscape photograph.

interval.label: Selected later hunting context, c. 1700–1850
interval.note: A bounded historical investigation, not the beginning of bison hunting or the site’s full chronology. UNESCO describes approximately 5800 BP to 1850 CE use with a lengthy hiatus. Earlier layers and later Blackfoot community histories are not compressed into these bounds.

question: How much coordinated work lies beyond the dramatic moment at the cliff?
summary: A communal bison hunt joined preparation, coordinated movement and the work of making food and materials usable. Blackfoot collaborative accounts connect the cliff with camp, fuel, water, drying and later hide work. This selected landscape and later historical window do not represent every Plains society or the beginning of bison knowledge.

sections.title: Preparation connected people, animals and a place
sections.text: The cliff was one part of a working landscape. UNESCO identifies drive lanes, bone deposits and processing camps as well as the escarpment. The Blackfoot/Glenbow collaborative exhibition explains why knowledge of bison behavior, wind and terrain mattered to preparation. A successful communal hunt depended on people acting together at the right moment. The material traces and public teaching account thus answer different parts of the same question: how a gathering of people could organize work across a much larger area than a photograph shows.

citations.locator: How We Lived with the Buffalo:campsite needs

sections.title: Coordination mattered before the animals reached the edge
sections.text: The collaborative account describes runners and others placed along drive lanes. Timing mattered: revealing people too early could turn a herd away. The interpretive-site history also describes organizations that regulated camp movement and communal hunting. These sources make planning and coordination visible without assuming a permanent farming settlement was required for social institutions. Their descriptions are situated interpretations, not a roster of one hunt or a fixed constitution shared by every Blackfoot group in every year.

sections.title: Processing changed the pace and kinds of work
sections.text: After the hunt, work continued quickly at the camp. The exhibition explains cutting meat for drying, removing hides carefully and obtaining fat from bones. These activities needed water, fuel and equipment, linking the choice of campsite to practical demands. Hide preparation required more time than removing a hide and was not always completed during the communal hunt. Drying and storage extended the use of food beyond the immediate event. This sequence makes processing a central achievement rather than an invisible task after the dramatic moment.

citations.locator: Work;Butchering and Drying Meat;Cutting Hides;Boiling Bones

sections.title: Seasonal work and respectful relations connected households
sections.text: The collaborative seasonal account places berry gathering, camp movement and preparing winter food within a wider round of activities. Blackfoot Crossing describes bison providing clothing, shelter and tools as well as food, and trade conducted through protocols of respect. The sources also place these practical relations within spiritual responsibilities. Public descriptions help a reader understand that connection; they do not transfer authority to reproduce ceremonies. The c.1700–1850 case is a selected later inquiry. Much earlier archaeological use, later photographs and continuing community knowledge keep their own dates.

claims.text: Head-Smashed-In includes drive lanes, a jump, bone deposits and processing camps; the landscape supports a history of coordinated hunting rather than an isolated cliff event.
claims.checkedBy: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval

returnPrompt: Draw or describe three kinds of work around a communal hunt. Separate what survives archaeologically from what needs other evidence.

deeperReading.title: Ask who made the teaching voice
deeperReading.text: The Glenbow project credits Blackfoot collaborators and distinguishes the website, teacher-toolkit and gallery teams. Its public English first person presents a collaborative teaching account; an unsigned sentence should not be assigned to one named contributor or made into an eighteenth-century quotation. The language page also notes the use of a Kainai version for many terms. Blackfoot Crossing provides a separately situated Siksika account. Read these voices with their attribution rather than blending them into a generic Plains speaker. Acknowledging public knowledge does not authorize copying every image, story or performance.

deeperReading.title: Let different evidence change the question
deeperReading.text: A modern surface photograph shows a cliff and grassland. It cannot expose buried processing deposits or tell us which individual carried out a task. Brink’s chapter 7 adds another method: a grease-processing experiment involving Piikani crew member Hazel Big Smoke, cattle bones and modern tools. Those conditions matter when judging what the experiment tests. It is neither an ancient meal nor an exact reenactment. Likewise, a modern painting or a later photograph captioned on the teaching website cannot silently become an image of the selected 1700–1850 case. What can the cliff, the experiment and the public Blackfoot teaching account each tell us about processing a hunt?

evidenceReading.title: Landscape, public teaching and a limited experiment
evidenceReading.introduction: Read the photograph, attributed public community teaching and the previously consulted experiment as different evidence. Their dates and methods cannot be collapsed into a photograph of one historical hunt.

items.label: A visible cliff is not the entire archaeological landscape
items.text: The modern photograph shows rock, grassland and a path. UNESCO separately identifies drive lanes, layered deposits and processing camps.
items.interpretation: The photograph can orient a viewer. It cannot by itself identify an ancient drive lane, expose buried layers or establish who used the site at every date.

items.label: Processing has its own sequence and resources
items.text: The collaborative camp account distinguishes quick processing and drying from the time-consuming preparation of hides, and relates the camp to water and fuel.
items.interpretation: This explains practical dependencies missing from a cliff-only story. It is a public teaching account rather than a labor census, exact recipe or individual witness to a dated event.

items.label: An experiment keeps its modern conditions
items.text: Brink’s selected account concerns bone/grease experiments involving Hazel Big Smoke, cattle bones and modern tools.
items.interpretation: The method can test practical interpretations. Replacing its materials or omitting the modern conditions would overstate what it establishes about every historical hunt.

familyActivity.title: Put the work beyond the cliff into the explanation
steps: Look at the photograph. Describe two visible features without assigning an ancient use to the modern path.
Read the supplied source capsule. Write down processing, drying and hide preparation as tasks described by that account.
Explain how one visible feature helps locate the setting and why one task needs a different source.
Write a supported claim and a further question. Do not stage a hunt, copy a ceremony or pretend to speak for a historical worker.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: This is a modern landscape photograph published in 2005, not a hunt in progress. The Blackfoot/Glenbow collaborative account describes quick processing at a camp, drying meat on frames and time-consuming preparation of hides. Water and fuel were also needed. These public teaching passages help explain work outside the photograph; they do not identify every historical worker or show buried archaeological layers. The activity asks for observation and source distinction; the supplied account provides its off-screen work evidence.

review.reviewer: Codex selected public-source consultation and internal author QA; not independent Blackfoot/community or historian acceptance
review.scope: Preparation, coordination, processing and seasonal work through public Blackfoot collaborative teaching and separately attributed Siksika interpretation. Four new selected source records; four precisely renewed inherited sources. Brink’s dated 27 October selected-page scope remains unaltered, without claiming a fresh full-book read. Whole original identity, 1700–1850 interval/note/claims/dimensions/terms and every media field/pixel remain exact. No map, annotation, asset or relationship added.
limitations: Public introductory cultural material is not permission to reproduce a ceremony, restricted story, song, design, performance or hunting reenactment. No such reproduction is supplied. The Glenbow copyright conditions and third-party rights remain explicit; no new image is licensed or copied here.

The collaborative exhibition does not assign every unsigned sentence to a named knowledge contributor. Its first-person narrative is not a recovered quotation from a dated 1700–1850 hunt, and the Kainai-oriented language choices are not made universal.
Brink chapter 7, printed pp. 195–198 is reused at its retained 27 October consultation scope. No new full-book/linked source/experimental replication or source-figure inspection is claimed.

Conflicting broad time/quantity generalizations on Blackfoot Crossing are not substituted for the qualified UNESCO site chronology or the original case dates. The approximate 1850 site boundary does not end community knowledge.

The existing photograph was actually viewed and its two files hashed. Source/publication/exposure distinctions and all rights/metadata remain untouched. No photo recovers every marker, buried layer, historical participant or entire hunt.

No precise new location, drive-lane survey, border or route is supplied. Independent historical/Blackfoot community review, family usability, accessibility/physical-device behavior and physical printing remain open; leaf checks cannot establish those acceptance tasks.
